title: Yahya bin Khalid and the Poor Man

keywords: yahya bin khalid and the poor man
full_text:
Yahya bin Khalid the Barmecide, renowned throughout Baghdad for his courtly refinement, was approached one afternoon by a modest, elderly scholar named Al-Hasan. The scholar was deeply versed in ancient poetry, philosophy, and history, but was so impoverished that his patched cloak barely concealed his frayed tunic.

Al-Hasan handed Yahya a sheet of parchment on which he had inscribed an elegant petition:
'My poverty is known to the heavens, yet my dignity forbids me to beg;
I knock upon the gate of Barmak, where generosity is the ancient law.'

Yahya read the verse with moist eyes. Instead of sending a servant with a purse of coins, which might have made the proud scholar feel like a common mendicant, Yahya stood from his divan, kissed the scholar’s forehead, and said: 'Welcome, venerable master! For months I have sought a scholar of your profound learning to catalog the rare manuscripts in my private library. Will you accept this office and honor my house with your presence?'

The scholar’s eyes filled with tears of gratitude; he had been offered not a humiliating handout, but an honorable office worthy of his intellect.

Yahya ordered a sum of two thousand gold dinars to be paid to Al-Hasan as his 'advance salary,' furnished him with a carriage, fine silk robes, and a comfortable house adjacent to the library.

For ten years, the scholar cataloged manuscripts, instructed Yahya’s sons, and lived in honored comfort.

Yahya’s companions marveled at his conduct, and Yahya replied: 'To give gold to a poor man while bruising his soul is cruelty disguised as charity. True generosity honors the mind and preserves the dignity of the receiver, so that both the giver and the recipient stand as brothers before the truth.'
moral: The highest charity preserves the self-respect of the recipient, treating him as an equal partner.
